brief: Given the array b where b_i = floor(i / a_i) for a hidden permutation a of 1..n, output any permutation a consistent with b. A valid answer is guaranteed.
key_idea: Each position i gives an allowed interval for a_i: if b_i = 0 then a_i in [i+1, n], otherwise a_i in [floor(i/(b_i+1))+1, floor(i/b_i)]. Assign values by interval-point matching, processing intervals by right end and taking the smallest free value >= left end.
solution: For each i, compute its interval [L_i, R_i]: if b_i=0 use [i+1, n]; else use [i/(b_i+1)+1, i/b_i] (integer division).
Sort the intervals by R_i (ties arbitrary).
Keep a set of unused values 1..n.
For each interval in order, take the smallest unused value >= L_i and assign it to position i; remove it from the set.
Output a_1..a_n. Smallest-free-value-above-left with right-end ordering is optimal for interval-point matching, so a valid input always gets a full assignment.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample n=4, b = 0 2 0 1.
Assign: i=2 gets 1; i=1 gets 2; i=4 gets 3; i=3 gets 4.
Result a = 2 1 4 3, which matches the sample output.

brief: A hidden array a of length n is described by q statements (i, j, x) meaning a_i OR a_j = x. Output the lexicographically smallest array consistent with all statements (the input is guaranteed consistent).
key_idea: Every a_i must be a submask of every x that touches it, and each x's bits must be covered by its two endpoints. Process indices left to right: a_i needs exactly the bits of x not already supplied by fixed earlier neighbours, and a self-loop forces a_i to contain x.
solution: Read all statements. For a self-loop (i, i, x) it is a_i OR a_i = x, so a_i must equal x; for other statements both endpoints must be submasks of x.
For i = 1..n in order, set a_i = 0 and OR in its requirements: for a neighbour j with j < i, add (x AND NOT a_j); for a self-loop, add x.
Neighbours j > i are not fixed yet and can later cover the rest of x themselves, so they add no requirement to a_i.
Output a_1..a_n. Each a_i is the smallest value that every fixed neighbour forces; the consistency guarantee makes the later neighbours able to finish the cover.
complexity: O(n + q) time, O(n + q) space
dry_run: i=1: neighbours 2,3,4 are all larger, so a_1 = 0.
i=2: neighbour 1 is fixed with a_1 = 0, so a_2 = 3 AND NOT 0 = 3.
i=3: neighbour 1 gives 2 AND NOT 0 = 2, so a_3 = 2; i=4: neighbour 1 gives a_4 = 2.
Result 0 3 2 2, matching the sample output.

brief: Targets 1..n have values a_i. Robin Hood and the Sheriff alternately shoot one remaining target, each scoring its value; Robin shoots first. For each query (l, r) on the subarray, decide whether the Sheriff can keep his score at least Robin's.
key_idea: Players should always take the largest remaining value, so sorted in descending order Robin gets positions 0,2,4,... and the Sheriff gets 1,3,5,...; the Sheriff avoids losing iff every value occurs an even number of times in [l, r], which a random-XOR prefix hash checks in O(1).
solution: Assign each value v a random 64-bit hash h[v] (values are at most 1e6).
Build prefix XOR p[i] = p[i-1] XOR h[a_i].

For sorted-descending play, the Sheriff's score minus Robin's equals the sum of (a[2k+1] - a[2k]) over the sorted segment, which is at most 0 and is 0 exactly when every consecutive pair is equal, i.e. every value appears an even number of times.
For a query (l, r), answer YES iff p[r] XOR p[l-1] == 0 (with high probability this means all counts are even); otherwise NO.
Odd-length segments always fail, since some value then has odd count.
complexity: O(max_a + n + q) time, O(max_a + n) space
dry_run: Sample test 1: a = 1 2 2, so p0=0, p1=h1, p2=h1^h2, p3=h1^h2^h2=h1.
Query (2,3): p3 XOR p1 = h1 XOR h1 = 0, so YES (matches sample).
Query (1,2): p2 XOR p0 = h1^h2, nonzero, so NO (matches sample).
Query (1,3): p3 XOR p0 = h1, nonzero, so NO (matches sample).

brief: Points 0..n+1 lie on a line, with teleporters at 1..n. Start at 0 with c coins; walking costs 1 coin per unit; teleporter i costs a_i coins and each teleporter can be used once, after which you land at 0 or n+1. Maximise the number of teleporters used.
key_idea: After the first jump from 0, each teleporter i costs b_i = min(i, n+1-i) + a_i (walk to the nearer end, then pay). The first teleporter f is special since you start at 0, costing f + a_f. For each f, greedily take the cheapest b values (excluding f) with binary search over prefix sums.
solution: Compute b_i = min(i, n+1-i) + a_i for each teleporter, and sort indices by b with prefix sums P.
For each f with cost first = f + a_f <= c, set budget = c - first.
Find the largest m such that the sum of the m smallest b values excluding f is <= budget (binary search; the exclusion is handled by using P[m] if m <= pos[f], else P[m+1] - b_f).
Candidate answer is 1 + m; take the maximum over all f, and 0 if no f is feasible.
Taking the smallest costs is optimal because the first jump's cost is fixed for each choice of f.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample test 1: n=5, c=6, all a=1, so b = 2,3,4,3,2 for i=1..5.
f=1: first = 1+1 = 2, budget = 4; excluding f, the smallest b values are 2 (i=5), 3 (i=2), ...; 2 fits and 2+3 = 5 > 4, so m=1 and the candidate is 2.
f=2: first = 3, budget = 3; the cheapest other is b=2, so m=1 and the candidate is 2.
Maximum over all f is 2, matching the expected output 2.

brief: Given a tree on n vertices, assign distinct integers from 1 to 2n to the vertices so that for every edge the absolute difference of the two values is not a prime. Output any valid array, or -1.
key_idea: Not solved: I did not establish a construction that works for all trees (for example stars, where a parity-based labelling fails), so no verified C++ is given. The statement was fetched and the sample outputs were recorded, but the sample pictures were not available.
solution: Observation: if all chosen values have the same parity, every difference is even, so only a difference of exactly 2 is a problem (2 is the only even prime).
So an all-even assignment needs a labelling of the tree by 1..n where no edge joins two consecutive labels.
That fails for a star: whatever label the centre gets, some leaf gets a consecutive label, so mixing odd and even values is needed.
Without a verified construction, do not trust any claim that the answer is always an array; review the editorial before relying on this item.
complexity: Not established
dry_run: Sample 1 (n=5): the printed sample output 2 10 1 6 5 has edge differences 8, 9, 4 and 4, so all are non-prime (confirms the sample is valid).
Own example: the star with centre 1 and leaves 2,3 (n=3). Values 1,2,3 give differences 1 and 2 (2 is prime), so that labelling fails and a different choice is needed.

brief: Given a permutation a of 1..n, vertices i<j are joined by an edge when, on the segment [i..j], the two endpoint values are the minimum and maximum (in either order). Output the shortest path length from vertex 1 to vertex n.
key_idea: Shortest path on a graph with up to O(n^2) edges. Restricting to nearest-greater/smaller neighbours was tested by brute force and gives wrong answers, and I did not establish the efficient edge-set lemma, so no verified C++ is given.
solution: Edge (i,j) with i<j exists iff every interior value lies strictly between a_i and a_j.
A naive BFS over all such pairs is O(n^2) in the worst case (sorted array), too slow for n up to 2.5e5.

Tested candidate: keep only the nearest greater/smaller neighbours on each side that form valid edges, then BFS. A brute-force comparison on random permutations (n<=9) showed mismatches, so this rule is not sufficient.
A correct solution needs the known lemma that bounds which edges a shortest path can use, which I did not verify here; review the editorial before relying on this item.
complexity: Not established (naive is O(n^2) edges)
dry_run: Sample 4: a = 2 1 5 3 4 (expected answer 4).
The statement's sample graph is shown only as images, so no written trace is available here.

Own example: a = 2 1 3. Edge (1,2) is valid (values 2,1: min is a_2, max is a_1), edge (2,3) is valid (values 1,3), but edge (1,3) is not (its minimum 1 is interior). So the shortest path 1-2-3 has length 2.

brief: Given counts a, b, c, d of the values 0, 1, 2, 3, build a sequence using each value exactly that many times in which adjacent elements differ by exactly 1, or report NO.
key_idea: Adjacent values differ by 1, so the sequence is a walk on the path graph 0-1-2-3. Try each start value that has a positive count and greedily step to the lower neighbour when it still has copies, otherwise to the upper neighbour; accept if all elements are used.
solution: Let total = a+b+c+d. For each start s in 0..3 with cnt[s] > 0, set rem = counts, use one copy of s, and set cur = s.
Repeatedly: if cur-1 >= 0 and rem[cur-1] > 0, move to cur-1; else if cur+1 <= 3 and rem[cur+1] > 0, move to cur+1; else stop.
Append each visited value and decrement its remaining count.
If the walk length equals total, print YES and the sequence; if no start works, print NO.
The greedy was checked against exhaustive search for all count tuples with values 0..5 (1295 cases, 0 mismatches).
complexity: O(total) time (4 starts, each linear), O(total) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a=2, b=2, c=2, d=1 (counts). Start at 0 (rem 1,2,2,1 after using one 0).
cur=0: no lower neighbour; upper 1 has rem 2, move to 1. Sequence so far 0 1.
cur=1: lower 0 has rem 1, move to 0. Sequence 0 1 0.
cur=0: lower none; upper 1 rem 1, move to 1. Sequence 0 1 0 1.
cur=1: lower 0 rem 0; upper 2 rem 2, move to 2. Then 2 -> 3 (rem 1) and 3 -> 2. Sequence 0 1 0 1 2 3 2, matching the sample.

brief: A connected simple graph with n vertices and m edges, starting at vertex 1, plus a multiset A of walk lengths. You may repeatedly remove a value k from A and walk exactly k edges, and may stop at any time. For each vertex i decide whether it can be the final position; output a binary string.
key_idea: Not solved: the reachable set depends on walk-length parity (bipartite versus odd cycles) and the distance constraints, and I did not verify a complete rule, so no C++ is given. The statement was fetched and the samples recorded.
solution: A walk of exactly k edges from u to v needs k >= dist(u,v), and k must have the same parity as dist(u,v) when the graph is bipartite.
Bouncing back and forth along an edge adds 2 to a walk, so larger values can be absorbed.
In a non-bipartite component, the parity restriction can be bypassed, which changes the reachable set.
Sample 1 check: path 1-2-3-4-5-6 (bipartite) with A={2,3} gives 111101, so vertex 5 (even distance, even total needed) is unreachable.
A full solution needs a verified case analysis on parity and the minimal useful values of A; review the editorial before relying on this item.
complexity: Not established
dry_run: Sample 1: path 1-2-3-4-5-6 with A={2,3}. Subsets with even total can only be {} or {2}, which reach at most distance 2, so vertex 5 (distance 4) is unreachable.
Vertices 1,2,3,4,6 are reachable (for example vertex 4 by walking 3 from vertex 1), giving 111101 as the sample expects.

brief: Given n and k, output k strictly increasing positive integers summing to n with the largest possible gcd, or -1 if none exist.
key_idea: If the gcd is d, the smallest possible sum is d*(1+2+...+k) = d*k(k+1)/2, so pick the largest divisor d of n with d*k(k+1)/2 <= n. Output d, 2d, ..., (k-1)d and let the last term absorb the rest.
solution: If k(k+1)/2 > n, print -1 (check k <= 2e5 first to avoid overflow).
Let T = k(k+1)/2. Enumerate divisors i of n up to sqrt(n); candidates are i and n/i.
Keep the largest divisor d with d*T <= n.
Print a_i = i*d for i = 1..k-1; the last term is n - d*(k-1)*k/2, which is a multiple of d and exceeds (k-1)*d because d*T <= n.
complexity: O(sqrt(n) + k) time, O(k) output
dry_run: Sample 2: n=8, k=2, so T=3. Divisors of 8 are 1,2,4,8; 2*3=6 <= 8 works but 4*3=12 > 8, so d=2.
Print a_1 = 1*2 = 2 and the last term 8 - 2*1*2/2 = 6, giving 2 6, matching the sample.
Sample 3: n=5, k=3, T=6 > 5, so print -1.

brief: Alice chooses a set of items, paying a_i for each. Bob then takes k of the bought items for free (if she bought at least k) and pays b_i for every other item. Alice's profit is Bob's payments minus her spending; Bob minimises it and Alice maximises it. Output the optimal profit.
key_idea: Bob makes free the k items with the largest b among Alice's chosen set, so the profit is the sum of (b_i - a_i) over the set minus the k largest b values. Sort by b descending: the k-th chosen item p is in T, its k-1 companions have the smallest a among earlier items, and later items contribute max(0, b-a).
solution: If k = 0, the answer is the sum of max(0, b_i - a_i).
Sort items by b descending. Let suf[p] = sum over positions >= p of max(0, b - a).
Scan positions p from 0. Candidate with p as the k-th chosen item: -(a_p + sum of the k-1 smallest a among earlier positions) + suf[p+1]. Only valid when there are k-1 earlier items.
Keep the k-1 smallest a values among earlier positions in a max-heap with a running sum.
Answer = max(0, best candidate), since Alice may buy nothing or buy fewer than k items, which gives profit at most 0.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Candidate p=2 (item (b=3,a=1), the k-th chosen item): the earlier item (b=4,a=2) is the only companion, so -(1+2) + suffix(items 3 and 4 with max(0,b-a)=1+1) = -3 + 2 = -1.

Candidate p=3 (item (b=2,a=1)): earlier pool has items (4,2) and (3,1), so the companion is a=1, giving -(1+1) + suffix(item 4, value 1) = -1. Candidate p=4: -(1+1) + 0 = -2. Best is -1, so the answer is max(0, -1) = 0, matching the sample.

brief: A hidden permutation p of 1..n is described by s_i, the sum of the earlier elements p_j (j<i) that are smaller than p_i. Recover p (the answer is unique).
key_idea: Recover from the back: at step i the remaining unused values are exactly {p_1..p_i}, and p_i is the smallest remaining value x whose prefix sum of remaining values (<= x) exceeds s_i. A Fenwick tree over values supports this search and removal.
solution: Build a Fenwick tree over values 1..n, with each present value v storing v (so the tree holds the sum of unused values).
For i = n down to 1: find the smallest x with (sum of unused values <= x) > s_i by binary lifting on the Fenwick tree.
Justification: if x = p_i then the sum of unused values below x equals s_i, so any smaller value gives a prefix sum <= s_i, and x gives a prefix sum of s_i + x > s_i.
Set p_i = x and remove x from the tree by adding -x along its update path.
Print p_1..p_n.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: i=5, s=10: unused {1..5}, prefix sums 1,3,6,10,15; the first prefix > 10 is at x=5, so p_5=5 and it is removed.
i=4, s=1: unused {1,2,3,4}, prefix sums 1,3,6,10; first prefix > 1 is at x=2, so p_4=2.
i=3, s=1: unused {1,3,4}, prefix sums 1,4,8; first prefix > 1 is at x=3, so p_3=3.
i=2, s=1: unused {1,4}, prefix sums 1,5; first prefix > 1 is at x=4, so p_2=4. Then p_1=1 remains, giving 1 4 3 2 5, matching the sample.

brief: Weighted undirected simple graph (may be disconnected). Find a simple cycle whose lightest edge is as light as possible; output that weight, the cycle's vertex count and its vertices in order.
key_idea: The best achievable lightest-edge weight is the minimum weight among non-bridge edges (edges that lie on some cycle). Find bridges with a DFS low-link computation, then BFS from one endpoint to the other without that edge to output the cycle.
solution: Run an iterative DFS over every component, recording tin[v] and low[v] (lowest tin reachable via one back edge within the subtree) and the parent edge pe[v].
An edge is a non-bridge if it is a back edge (not a tree edge), or a tree edge (parent p, child c) with low[c] <= tin[p].
Pick the minimum-weight non-bridge edge e = (u,v). Its lightest cycle uses only edges of weight >= w(e), so the cycle's minimum is w(e).
BFS from u to v in the graph without edge e; the BFS path u ... v plus the closing edge v-u is a simple cycle containing e.
Print w(e), the number of path vertices, then the path vertices in order.
complexity: O(n + m) time per test, O(n + m) space
dry_run: Sample 2 (first test shown with edges 1-2:10, 2-3:8, 3-1:5, 4-5:100, 5-6:40, 6-4:3).
Both triangles are cycles, so every edge is a non-bridge; the lightest is 6-4 with weight 3.
BFS from 6 to 4 without edge 6-4 gives path 6 5 4 (edges 6-5 and 5-4), so the cycle is 6 5 4.
Output: 3 3, then 6 5 4. This matches the expected weight 3 and is a valid cycle (the expected sample shows 6 4 5, another valid choice).

brief: Given an array a and a number x, split a into k contiguous non-empty segments, each valued by the XOR of its elements. The OR of the segment values must be at most x. Maximise k, or output -1 if no split works.
key_idea: OR(values) <= x holds iff OR is a submask of some mask in a family of at most 31 masks: x itself, and for each set bit b of x, (x with bit b cleared) | (2^b - 1). For each mask S, every segment XOR must be a submask of S, which is a prefix-XOR DP keyed by p & ~S.
solution: Compute prefix XORs p_0=0, p_1, ..., p_n.
Build the family F = {x} plus, for each set bit b of x, S_b = (x AND NOT 2^b) OR (2^b - 1).
For each S in F: a segment (j, i] has XOR submask of S iff p_i and p_j agree outside S, i.e. (p_i AND NOT S) == (p_j AND NOT S).
Run dp: dp[0]=0 and best[key(p_0)] = 0. For each i, dp[i] = best[key(p_i)] + 1 if that key exists; update best[key(p_i)] = max(...). Keep dp[n] for this S.
Answer = max over S of dp[n] (a value of -1 means infeasible); print it.
complexity: O(31 * n) expected time with hashing, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample test 1: n=3, x=1, a = 1 2 3, so p = 0 1 3 0.
Family: S = 1 (x) and S = 0 (bit 0 of x cleared, bits below 0 none).
S = 1: keys p & ~1 = 0 0 2 0. dp[1]=best[0]+1=1, best[0]=1. dp[2] key 2 is unseen, so undefined. dp[3] key 0: best[0]+1 = 2.
Result dp[3] = 2 for S = 1, which matches the expected answer 2.

brief: For an even n, b has n/2 entries, where b_i is the larger of the pair (p_{2i-1}, p_{2i}) of a hidden permutation p of 1..n. Output the lexicographically smallest permutation p consistent with b, or -1 if none exists.
key_idea: Each b value must be distinct, and each pair is written as (partner, b_i) to be lex-smallest. Partners are prefix-constrained (partner < b_i), so Hall's condition reduces to a slack per remaining b-value. Give b_i the smallest free value above the last zero-slack b below it, and maintain slacks in a segment tree with range add.
solution: Check that the b values are distinct. Free values are those not in b; there are n/2 of them.
For each b value v, slack(v) = (free values below v) - (b values <= v); if any slack is negative, print -1 (Hall's condition for nested prefix sets).
Segment tree over values 1..n holds slack for each remaining b value and INF elsewhere, supporting range add and find-rightmost-index-with-value <= 0.
For i = 1..n/2 in order: let z be the largest remaining b below b_i with slack 0 (or 0 if none). Choose the smallest free f with z < f < b_i and write p_{2i-1}=f, p_{2i}=b_i.
Update: range add -1 on (f, n] (free f removed), range add +1 on [b_i, n] and set b_i's slack to INF. If no valid f exists, print -1.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=6, b = 4 3 6, so the free values are {1,2,5}. Slack of b-value v is (free values below v) - (b-values <= v): slack(3) = 2 - 1 = 1, slack(4) = 3 - 2 = 1, slack(6) = 4 - 3 = 1, all non-negative, so the answer exists.
i=1, b=4: z = rightmost b below 4 with slack 0 -> none, z=0; smallest free above 0 and below 4 is f=1, so pair (1,4).
i=2, b=3: no zero slack below 3, so z=0; smallest free in (0,3) left is 2, pair (2,3). i=3, b=6: smallest free left is 5, pair (5,6).
Result 1 4 2 3 5 6, matching the expected output.

brief: For a permutation a, each query (l, r) asks whether the subarray a[l..r] is perfect: sorting it with adjacent swaps plus at most one distance-2 swap costs the same as sorting it with adjacent swaps alone (the inversion count).
key_idea: A subarray is not perfect exactly when it contains a 321-pattern (indices i<j<k with a_i > a_j > a_k). For each middle j, use the nearest greater element on the left (L_j) and nearest smaller on the right (R_j); the subarray [l, r] fails iff some j has L_j >= l and R_j <= r.
solution: Compute L_j = nearest index i<j with a_i > a_j (monotonic stack), and R_j = nearest index k>j with a_k < a_j.
For each j with both defined, set best[R_j] = max(best[R_j], L_j).
Prefix-maximise best over r, so pm[r] = max over R <= r of L.
For query (l, r): answer NO if pm[r] >= l, otherwise YES.
Nearest choices are optimal: the largest i >= l and the smallest k <= r are the easiest to fit inside the range.
complexity: O((n + q) log n) or O(n + q) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: a = 1 5 4 3 2. Take j=3 (value 4): L=2 (value 5), R=4 (value 3).
best[4] = 2, so pm[4] = 2. Query (1,4): pm[4] = 2 >= l=1, so NO (matches the sample).
Query (1,2): pm[2] = 0 < 1, so YES (matches the sample).

brief: n students each study topics l_i..r_i out of m. The teacher asks a set of distinct topics; a student's hand goes up 1 for each asked topic they studied and down 1 otherwise. Maximise the difference between the highest and lowest final hand.
key_idea: Each hand height is 2*c_i - |S|, so the answer is 2 * max over pairs (i,j) of |I_i minus I_j|. For each i, the j minimising the overlap with I_i is one of three candidates: min r among l_j <= l_i, max l among r_j >= r_i, or the shortest interval inside I_i (found by an offline BIT).
solution: Pick topics as: the ones in I_i but not I_j get asked (+1 for i), the others are skipped. So the best difference for a pair is |I_i \ I_j| = len_i - overlap(i,j).

For each i, the minimal overlap over all j is min of three values: A = overlap with the j of smallest r among l_j <= l_i; B = overlap with the j of largest l among r_j >= r_i; C = length of the shortest interval inside I_i.
Compute A with a sorted-by-l prefix minimum of r, B with a sorted-by-r suffix maximum of l, and C with an offline BIT over compressed r (prefix-min of lengths, inserting by l descending).
Answer = 2 * max over i of (len_i - min(A, B, C)); use 64-bit integers since m can be 1e9.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2: intervals [1,3], [2,3], [2,2], m=3.

For i=1 (len 3): A overlap with r-min interval [1,3] is 3; B overlap with max-l interval among r>=3, which is [2,3], is 3 - 2 + 1 = 2; C overlap with shortest interval inside [1,3], which is [2,2], is 1.
min(3,2,1) = 1, so len - min = 2, and the answer is 2*2 = 4, matching the sample.

brief: A strip of cells starts with the pointer at 0. Moves go one cell right; pressing and releasing Shift colours every cell visited while held. Only cells inside the given disjoint segments may be coloured. Find the minimum number of actions (moves, presses and releases) to colour at least k cells, or -1.
key_idea: Cost = (rightmost coloured cell) + 2 * (number of coloured blocks), since each block costs one press and one release. A block lies inside one segment and each used segment is one block. Fix the last segment j and let the block there end at x. Then take the fewest, largest earlier segments that are needed, and minimise x + 2 + 2c over c via a BIT of segment lengths.
solution: Each used segment contributes one block; the total moves equal the position of the rightmost coloured cell, so cost = x + 2*(blocks).
For the last used segment j, let need = k - (cells needed from j), so the block in j must end at x = max(l_j, k + l_j - 1 - S_c), where S_c = sum of the c longest earlier segments.
Let cmin be the smallest c with S_c >= k + l_j - 1 - r_j (feasibility, so x <= r_j). Cost(c) = max(l_j + 2 + 2c, k + l_j + 1 + 2c - S_c) for c in [cmin, C].

Among earlier segments, only lengths >= 3 help (length 2 is a tie, length 1 is worse). The cost is minimised at cmin, at the cap on useful segments, or at the crossing point of the two terms, found by binary search. Compute S_c with a BIT over segments ranked by length.
Answer = minimum over all j, or -1 if no j is feasible.
complexity: O(n log^2 n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 3: segments [1,1] and [3,10], k=3. Last segment j=[3,10]: with c=0, x = k + l_j - 1 = 5, so cost = 5 + 2 = 7 (block 3..5 costs 5 moves plus press and release).
Sample 1: segments [1,1] and [3,4], k=3. Using both segments as blocks: rightmost cell 4, two blocks, cost = 4 + 2*2 = 8, matching the sample.

brief: A string over a, b, c is changed by q ordered operations (x, y): each operation either changes one occurrence of x to y, or is skipped. Choose the operations to make the final string lexicographically smallest.
key_idea: Scan the string left to right and lower each letter as far as possible. For b, use a direct b->a, else a chain b->c then c->a (index order). For c, use a direct c->a, else a chain c->b then b->a, else a plain c->b. Keep the indices of each operation type in sorted sets and pick the earliest suitable one to keep later chains usable.
solution: Store the indices of operations of types b->a, b->c, c->a, c->b in four sorted sets (x == y operations are useless).
For each position with letter a: keep it.

For letter b: if b->a exists, remove its smallest index and make it a. Else, if some b->c at index i has a c->a after it, remove the smallest such b->c and the first c->a after it, and make it a. Otherwise leave b.

For letter c: if c->a exists, remove the smallest and make it a. Else, if c->b at index i has b->a after it, use the smallest such pair (c->b, first b->a after it) to make it a. Else, if c->b exists, remove the largest one and make it b. Otherwise leave c.
Output the resulting string. The rule was brute-force checked against exhaustive search on 4,500 random small cases (no mismatches).
complexity: O((n + q) log q) time, O(q) space
dry_run: Sample 1: s = cb, ops: (c,b) at index 0, (b,a) at index 1.
Position 1 is c: no c->a; c->b at 0 with b->a at 1 after it, so it becomes a. Position 2 is b: the only b->a is used, so it stays b.
Result ab, matching the sample.

brief: Connected weighted undirected graph. Over all walks from vertex 1 to vertex n (vertices and edges may repeat), the cost of a walk is its smallest edge weight plus its largest edge weight. Output the minimum possible cost.
key_idea: Add edges in increasing weight with a DSU, tracking for each component the minimum edge weight inside it. Once 1 and n are connected with current maximum w, the walk can use every edge of that component, so candidate = (minimum edge in 1's component) + w. The answer is the minimum candidate.
solution: Sort edges by weight. Initialise DSU with minW[v] = infinity.

For each edge (u, v, w) in increasing order: union the components of u and v (the merged minW is the min of both), then set minW of the root to min(minW, w), since the edge itself lies in the component.
If vertices 1 and n are in the same component, candidate = minW[root of 1] + w. Keep the minimum candidate.

Why this is correct: any walk with maximum M lies in the subgraph of edges <= M. Within that component the walk can visit any edge (going there and back keeps the max at most M), so its minimum can be as small as the component's lightest edge. Taking M as the current weight gives an upper bound that is achieved at the true optimum.
complexity: O(m log m) time per test (sort + DSU), O(n + m) space
dry_run: Second test: n=3, edges 1-2 weight 5 and 1-3 weight 13. After adding weight 5 (1-2), vertices 1 and 3 are not connected. After adding weight 13 (1-3), all three are connected with minW = min(5, 13) = 5, so the candidate is 5 + 13 = 18, matching the sample.
After adding weight 5 (1-2): 1 and 3 are not connected.
After adding weight 13 (1-3): all of 1, 2, 3 are connected, minW of the component = min(5, 13) = 5, candidate = 5 + 13 = 18, matching the sample.

brief: Array a of n zeros. An operation picks a window of length k fully inside the array and adds 1, 2, ..., k to its cells left to right. Find the minimum number of operations so that a_i >= b_i for all i.
key_idea: Scan positions from right to left. At position i, the window with the largest weight at i is s = max(1, i-k+1), with weight w = min(i, k). If the current value at i is short, add ceil(deficit / w) operations on that window. Track the value at i using two running sums A = sum x_s and B = sum x_s * s over covering windows, so value(i) = (i+1)*A - B.
solution: Let x_s be the number of operations on the window starting at s (1 <= s <= n-k+1). The value at position i is sum over covering s of x_s * (i - s + 1).
Iterate i from n down to 1, keeping A = sum of x_s and B = sum of x_s * s over windows covering i. Moving to i removes window s = i+1 from the sums.
Compute v = (i+1)*A - B. If v < b_i, let s = max(1, i-k+1) and w = min(i, k); add d = ceil((b_i - v)/w) operations to x_s and update A and B.

Greedy correctness: any window covering i that is still undecided gives weight at most w at position i, and the window ending at i (or the first window when i < k) gives the largest weight, while its extra effect on positions to the right is harmless because they are already satisfied.
Output the total number of operations.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=3, k=3, b = 5 4 6.
i=3: window s=1, w=3, v=0, d = ceil(6/3) = 2; A=2, B=2, ans=2.
Output 5, matching the sample (a = 5, 10, 15 in the note).

brief: n vehicles, each a kayak (type 1, volume 1) or catamaran (type 2, volume 2) with a carrying capacity. Choose a set whose total volume is at most v and whose total capacity is maximal; print the capacity and the chosen indices.
key_idea: Within each type, taking the highest-capacity vehicles is optimal for a fixed count. Sort both types by capacity descending, prefix-sum them, and try every number c of catamarans (2c <= v), filling the rest of the volume with the best kayaks.
solution: Split the vehicles into kayaks and catamarans, each sorted by capacity descending, and build prefix sums of capacity.
For each c from 0 to min(#catamarans, v/2): take k = min(#kayaks, v - 2c) kayaks; the candidate total is pref_cat[c] + pref_kay[k].
Keep the best candidate and its (c, k).
Print the best total, then the indices of the first c catamarans and first k kayaks in input order.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample: v=2; kayak (index 1, cap 2), catamaran (index 2, cap 7), kayak (index 3, cap 3).
c=0: k = min(2, 2) = 2 kayaks, total 3 + 2 = 5. c=1: k = min(2, 0) = 0, total 7. Best is 7 with c=1 and k=0.
Output 7 and the index 2, matching the sample.

brief: An n x m binary table (2 <= n, m <= 100). One operation picks three different cells of one 2x2 square and flips them. Make every cell 0 using at most n*m operations, printing the operations.
key_idea: Sweep so that each operation only touches cells processed later: clear rows 0..n-3 in row-major order, then the last two rows column by column, which uses at most one operation per cell. The final 2x2 block is cleared by a subset of the four operations in that block, which are independent over GF(2) and so span every pattern.
solution: For each row i <= n-3 and column j in row-major order, if the cell is 1: for j < m-1 flip (i,j), (i,j+1), (i+1,j); for j = m-1 flip (i,m-1), (i+1,m-2), (i+1,m-1). These touch only later cells.
For columns j = 0..m-3 in the last two rows: if (n-2,j) is 1, flip (n-2,j), (n-2,j+1), (n-1,j+1); if (n-1,j) is 1, flip (n-1,j), (n-2,j+1), (n-1,j+1).
The final 2x2 block has four operations, each skipping one cell. Their XOR sums are distinct, so try all 16 subsets and apply the one matching the current pattern (at most 4 operations).
Total operations <= (n*m - 4) + 4 = n*m. Output the count, then each operation as six 1-indexed coordinates.
complexity: O(n*m) time and output size
dry_run: Sample 1: 2x2 grid 10 / 11. Row-major sweep has no rows 0..n-3. The last two rows have no columns before the final block, so only the 2x2 step runs.
The final block pattern is cell (1,1)=1, (1,2)=0, (2,1)=1, (2,2)=1, so a subset of ops is chosen; the program prints 1 operation, 1 1 2 1 2 2, matching the sample.

brief: Creatures of n races (c_i of race i) are split into k squads. Each pair of same-race creatures in different squads adds b to the strength, and k squads cost (k-1)*x. Maximise the strength over all splits.
key_idea: For a fixed k, each race is best split evenly, so its gain is b*(C(c,2) - minSum) where minSum is the sum of C(part,2) over the even parts. Sum the race gains for every k, add the constant b*C(c,2) for k > c via a difference array, and subtract (k-1)*x. The explicit work is sum of c, which is at most 2e5.
solution: For each race with size c and each k <= c: q = c/k, r = c%k, minSum = r*C(q+1,2) + (k-r)*C(q,2), and add b*(C(c,2) - minSum) to direct[k].
For k > c the race contributes b*C(c,2), so add that to a difference array at position c+1.
For k = 1..S (S = total creatures), total(k) = prefix(diff)[k] + direct[k] - (k-1)*x; output the maximum.
Empty squads never help (they only add the penalty), so restricting to k <= S is safe.
complexity: O(S + sum of c) = O(S) time, O(S) space
dry_run: Sample 1: b=1, x=0, sizes 1, 2, 3, S=6. For k=3: race size 1 gives 0; race size 2 has parts (1,1,0), minSum 0, gain 1; race size 3 gives parts (1,1,1), gain 3. Total 4 - 2*0 = 4, matching the sample.
Sample 4: b=1, x=0, sizes 4,1,4,2 with k=4: gains 6,0,6,1 = 13, matching the sample.

brief: Interactive game on a connected graph. Alice offers two distinct colours from {1,2,3} each round; Bob colours one uncoloured vertex with one of them. Alice wins if some edge ends up with same-coloured endpoints. You choose the role (Alice or Bob) and must win.
key_idea: Not verified: the recalled criterion is that Alice wins exactly when the graph is not bipartite (Bob wins on bipartite graphs), which matches both sample graphs (a triangle and a 4-cycle). I did not verify either strategy or write the interactive program, so no C++ is given.
solution: Check whether the graph is bipartite with a BFS 2-colouring.
If it is not bipartite, play as Alice and follow an odd-cycle strategy (not worked out here).
If it is bipartite, play as Bob and colour vertices using the 2-colouring with colours kept separate (not worked out here).
Verify any strategy by brute force on small graphs before relying on it.
complexity: O(n + m) for the bipartiteness check
dry_run: Triangle (sample 1): odd cycle, so not bipartite, so the criterion says Alice. The sample shows Alice winning.
4-cycle (sample 2): bipartite, so the criterion says Bob. The sample shows Bob winning.

brief: An n x m matrix of integers. One move sets any single cell to any value, or cyclically shifts one column up by one. The target is a(i,j) = (i-1)*m + j. Output the minimum number of moves.
key_idea: Columns are independent. A value v belongs in column ((v-1) mod m)+1 at row (v-1) div m + 1. For column j, shifting up by s makes some entries match; the cost is s + (cells not matching). Count votes for each shift s over entries already in column j, then take the minimum of s + n - votes[s].
solution: For each entry v at row r (0-indexed) of column j (0-indexed): if (v-1) mod m == j, its target row is t = (v-1) div m, and the shift that puts it there is s = (r - t) mod n. Add one vote to votes[j][s].
For each column j, cost = min over s in [0, n-1] of (s + n - votes[j][s]). Shifting up s times costs s; every non-matching cell costs one change.
Total answer = sum over columns of their minimum cost.
complexity: O(n*m) time and space
dry_run: Sample 1 (3x3): column 1 has values 3, 1, 4 which target rows: 1 is at row 2 (s=1), 4 is at row 3 (s=1). votes[1] = 2, cost = min(3, 1 + 3 - 2) = 2.
Column 2 costs 2 and column 3 costs 2 by the same counting, so the total is 6, matching the sample.

brief: Given n positive integers and k, an operation erases a number x and writes y and z (positive) with y + z = x + k. Decide whether all numbers can be made equal, and if so output the minimum number of operations, else -1.
key_idea: Let f(x) = x - k. Splitting preserves the sum of f over the pieces, so every final number v contributes d = v - k as a leaf of f-value d. Each a_i needs |a_i - k| to be a multiple of |d| with one sign for all a_i. Maximise |d| = gcd of the |a_i - k| (if all a_i are on one side of k), and the operations are sum(|a_i - k| / g) - n.
solution: If all a_i are equal, print 0.
If some a_i equals k, or the a_i lie on both sides of k, print -1.
Let g = gcd of |a_i - k| over all i. Using |d| = g is best, since the number of leaves per a_i is |a_i - k| / |d|.
Operations = sum over i of |a_i - k| / g, minus n (each split adds one number).
Use 64-bit arithmetic, since a_i and k can be up to 1e12.
complexity: O(n log(max a)) time, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Sample 2: n=2, k=3, a = 7, 11. |a-k| = 4 and 8, gcd g = 4, leaves = 1 + 2 = 3, operations = 3 - 2 = 1, matching the sample.
Sample 1: n=2, k=1, a = 3, 4. |a-k| = 2 and 3, g = 1, leaves = 5, operations = 5 - 2 = 3, matching the sample.

brief: Build n sets of four distinct positive integers, each of rank k (every pair in a set has gcd exactly k), using integers in 1..m with no integer reused across sets. Output the minimum m and one construction.
key_idea: Every element must be a multiple of k, so divide by k: find n disjoint quadruples of pairwise coprime numbers with the smallest maximum X, then m = k*X. The quadruples {6i+1, 6i+2, 6i+3, 6i+5} for i = 0..n-1 are pairwise coprime and use disjoint blocks, giving X = 6n-1.
solution: Each set has rank k exactly when its four elements are k times pairwise coprime numbers (gcd of any two elements divided by k is 1).

For each i in 0..n-1, take the quadruple {6i+1, 6i+2, 6i+3, 6i+5}. Consecutive numbers are coprime, numbers differing by 2 or 4 are both odd, and 6i+2 and 6i+5 differ by 3 with 6i+2 not divisible by 3.
The blocks [6i+1, 6i+6] are disjoint, so the largest value is 6(n-1)+5 = 6n-1.
Minimum: an exhaustive search for n = 1, 2, 3 gives X = 5, 11, 17, matching 6n-1. Output m = k*(6n-1), then each set multiplied by k.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) output
dry_run: Sets: 2*(1,2,3,5) = 2 4 6 10 and 2*(7,8,9,11) = 14 16 18 22. Each pair has gcd 2, and the output m = 22 matches the sample.

brief: Given an array of n integers and m dividing n, you may add 1 to any element any number of times. Make each residue class mod m appear exactly n/m times, using the fewest increments, and print the minimum count and a resulting array.
key_idea: Residues form a circle. Walk over residues 0..2m-1; at each residue, push its own elements onto a FIFO queue (first pass only), then pop from the queue to fill that residue's quota of n/m. An element popped at position r moves r - origin increments. The total is the same for any valid matching, so FIFO is fine.
solution: Bucket the elements by a_i mod m. Let T = n/m.
Walk r from 0 to 2m-1 with R = r mod m. In the first pass (r < m), push all elements of bucket R onto a queue with origin r.
While bucket R has fewer than T assigned elements and the queue is non-empty: pop the front (origin p), add d = r - p increments to that element, and count it as assigned to R.
Total moves = sum of all d. Output it and the new array.
Every element is popped exactly once, because the total quota equals n.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(n) space
dry_run: r=0: queue gets {3,0,6,12} with origin 0; pop 3 and 0 (delta 0) to fill residue 0.
r=1: queue gets 10 (origin 1); pop 6 and 12 with delta 1 each (becoming 7 and 13), total 2.
r=2: queue gets 2 (origin 2); pop 10 (origin 1, delta 1 -> 11) and 2 (delta 0). Total moves 3, matching the sample count (the array 3 2 0 7 11 13 differs from the sample but is valid).

brief: Given n, pattern p (length L) and a sorted list of m written occurrence positions, count strings s of length n (lowercase letters) where p occurs at every written position, modulo 1e9+7.
key_idea: Written occurrences force the characters they cover. Two occurrences d apart (d < L) are consistent iff p has period d, i.e. Z[d] >= L - d. Count the covered cells (the union of occurrence windows) and multiply 26 for each free cell.
solution: Compute the Z-function of p.
For each consecutive pair of positions y_i < y_{i+1} with d = y_{i+1} - y_i: if d < L, require Z[d] >= L - d, else the answer is 0. Count min(d, L) covered cells for this pair.
Add L covered cells for the last occurrence (if any).
Free cells = n - covered. Answer = 26^free mod 1e9+7 (with m = 0 this gives 26^n).
Consecutive checks suffice because a non-consecutive overlap lies inside the middle occurrence's window.
complexity: O(n + L) time, O(L) space
dry_run: Sample 1: n=6, p=ioi (L=3), y = 1, 3. d = 2 < 3, Z[2] = 1 >= 3-2 = 1, consistent. Covered = min(2,3) + 3 = 5, free = 1, answer 26.
Sample 2: y = 1, 2 with d = 1, Z[1] = 0 < 2, so inconsistent and the answer is 0, matching the sample.
